summary: Offers guidance on when IPsec version 2 should and should not be specified in Internet specifications, since just use IPsec in a Security Considerations section often leaves users without real, interoperable security. This is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: Writers often say just use the lock called IPsec. This memo warns that it is not always the right lock and helps writers choose well.

questions: when to specify ipsec in a protocol
is just use ipsec good security advice
transport mode vs tunnel mode ipsec
subtitle: Why writing 'just use IPsec' in a specification is not enough, and what a spec must say if it does choose IPsec.

tldr.problem: Many Internet Drafts say in their Security Considerations, in effect, 'just use IPsec', which often leaves users without real, interoperable security.
tldr.mechanism: The memo walks through IPsec version 2 pieces (AH, ESP, modes, key management, APIs, selectors) and their practical limits, then lists nine things a specification must state if it relies on IPsec, with a BGP example.
tldr.outcome: Protocol designers get a checklist for deciding whether to use IPsec and for specifying it precisely. It covers IPsec version 2 only; IPsec version 3 is left to a separate document.

today: RFC 5406 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 146) and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It covers IPsec version 2 only; the text says IPsec version 3 would be handled in a separate document.

sections.title: The Problem With Just Use IPsec
sections.content:
If IPsec is unavailable to a majority of the users in a protocol environment, requiring it is tantamount to saying 'turn off security' for that community. Even where IPsec exists, it may not give the right granularity of protection, and a document that mandates it must say just how it is to be used.

This memo covers IPsec version 2: the architecture in RFC 2401, ESPv2, AHv2 and IKEv1. A separate document is to describe IPsec version 3. It also warns that the design of security protocols is a subtle and difficult art. Rejecting IPsec does not mean inventing a new protocol; another standardized, well-understood protocol will almost always give better results.
sections.eli5: Saying 'use the strong lock' is useless if most doors cannot hold it. And do not build your own lock, because homemade locks are usually worse.

sections.title: The Pieces of IPsec
sections.content:
The Authentication Header (AH) and the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) are the over-the-wire protocols. Both offer optional replay protection. ESP usually gives confidentiality, integrity and authentication, and can give integrity without confidentiality, which makes it a good alternative to AH in most cases. ESP alone for confidentiality is possible but not recommended. AH is needed only if an application requires protection of parts of the IP header or of IP options, which the RFC calls extremely rare. If confidentiality is required, ESP must be used.

All IPsec variants have problems with NAT boxes, and AH has considerably more. Where endpoints are likely to be separated by a NAT, which covers almost all user-to-server traffic, NAT traversal (RFC 3948) should be mandated and AH avoided. That NAT traversal works for ESP only.

In tunnel mode an inner IP header follows the IPsec header. It is the normal choice for VPNs and is generally needed whenever one end is not the final IP destination. Transport mode is preferred for point-to-point communication.
sections.eli5: IPsec has two kinds of envelopes. One seals the letter and checks it was not changed, and the other only checks it was not changed. Routers that rewrite addresses confuse the second kind more.

sections.title: Key Management and Certificates
sections.content:
IPsec supports manual and automatic key management. Manual keying is easy but does not scale, and replay protection is not available with it. The main automatic mechanism is IKE (RFC 2409). Kerberized Internet Negotiation of Keys (KINK) exists too, but suits only sites with a Kerberos infrastructure.

IKE can run in main mode or aggressive mode, with digital signatures, public key encryption or shared secrets. Shared secrets are simpler but scale poorly when many parties talk to many parties, yet they are still far preferable to manual keying.

The memo is blunt about certificates: there is no global PKI covering most Internet endpoints and probably never will be, so designing around one is a mistake. Public key IKE is generally good but should almost always use locally issued certificates. Public key schemes also cost computation; certificates roughly double the number of large exponentiations compared with shared secret IKE, and busy concentration points such as firewalls or VoIP servers may need hardware assistance.

Automatic keying can be impossible for low-level protocols. RFC 2461 called for IPsec to protect IPv6 Neighbor Discovery, but IKE needs IP-level communication, which is not possible before Neighbor Discovery associations exist.
sections.eli5: Swapping secret keys by hand works for two friends but not for a whole school. Using a computer to swap them is better, though it takes more effort from the machines.

sections.title: Availability, Endpoints and Granularity
sections.content:
IPsec is widely implemented in host operating systems but less so in embedded systems. Few hubs or network address translators support it, especially at the low end, so relying on it is generally inappropriate when many endpoints are in that category. Hosts that support IPsec for VPN use often do not support it point to point, and few support multiple layers of IPsec, so a telecommuter in a VPN may be unable to add a second layer for one application.

There is also no portable API: applications rarely can request IPsec, check that it was used, or see the identity of the protected channel. Higher-layer services such as TLS give that control. User-level identification is not common, and some implementations cannot use port numbers in their selectors, so protection is all-or-nothing between two hosts. The selectors in the Security Policy Database (SPD) can name addresses, protocol numbers (6 for TCP, 17 for UDP) and ports. Traffic inside an L2TP session cannot be selected by IPsec above L2TP for lack of selectors.

Multicast protection was not completed until much later, so many implementations lack it; RFC 5374 describes extensions.
sections.eli5: Not every device can use the fancy lock, and apps cannot easily ask for it or check it. Often it is all doors or no doors.

sections.title: What a Specification Must Say
sections.content:
If IPsec is still the right choice, authors MUST define precisely how it is used. The memo lists nine questions:

  • Which selectors the initiator uses (addresses, ports and so on).
  • AH or ESP, and transport or tunnel mode.
  • What form of key management.
  • What form of identification: IP address, DNS name with or without a user name, or X.500 distinguished name.
  • Whether a new security association is negotiated if a server switches user IDs.
  • What authentication: pre-shared secrets or certificates.
  • How participants are authorized.
  • Which IKE variants are required (main or aggressive mode), and which version, IKE or IKEv2.
  • Whether suitable IPsec support exists in the likely products.
sections.eli5: If you do choose the lock, write down which lock, which key, who gets keys and which doors. Leave nothing to guessing.

sections.title: Worked Example: BGP
sections.content:
The memo applies the checklist to the Border Gateway Protocol, without claiming IPsec is the right choice for it. BGP runs between manually configured pairs of hosts on TCP port 179, so the selector is the pair of speakers for that port. Transport mode fits, and since the data is generally not confidential, encryption need not be used; AH or ESP must be mandated for interoperability. Automated key management such as IKE is advised to permit replay detection.

Authentication is harder: large ISPs have so many routers that shared keys are likely inadequate, so certificate-based IKE must be supported, though shared secrets may do on peering links. The key question is availability: whether BGP speakers support the profile, and whether expensive cryptography opens new denial-of-service attacks.
sections.eli5: The memo practices on one real job, routers talking to routers, to show how to answer each question one at a time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: IPsec provides transmission security and simple access control only. It does little against denial-of-service attacks and on CPU-limited systems may contribute to them. The security of a resulting protocol depends heavily on how accurate the analysis was that led to choosing IPsec.
sections.eli5: The lock keeps messages safe in transit, but it cannot stop someone from jamming the door.
